Authors: We sincerely thank you for these insightful questions regarding the relationship
between saccadic eye movements and their possible visual consequences, that are indeed
critical to understanding avian vision.
First, we would like to clarify that “saccades” and “oscillatory saccades” are not differentiated
eye movement types in birds. In pigeons, each saccade comprises both a displacement in eye
position and several cycles of oscillation, as previously reported and confirmed by our long-
term studies. Whether during spontaneous saccades (Pettigrew et al., 1990; Wallman & Letelier,
1993; Yang Yang et al., 2008) or the quick phase of optokinetic nystagmus (Xiao et al., 2023;
Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang Yang et al., 2008), oscillations consistently appear as an intrinsic
component of every saccade rather than a separate movement category. We apologize for the
misleading terminology in the previous submission. In the revised manuscript, we now use
“saccade” when referring to the overall saccadic eye movement and “saccadic oscillation” or
“oscillation” when emphasizing its oscillatory component. Figure 1 has been updated
accordingly to illustrate these features of avian saccades more clearly.
Second, we agree with you that these oscillations could blur the retinal image during saccadic
eye movements. However, our previous work demonstrated that saccades in pigeons induce
perisaccadic inhibition of neuronal firing in the brain visual regions during saccades, mediated
by corollary discharge signals from brainstem neurons (Yan Yang et al., 2008). This suppression
mechanism likely contributes to visual stabilization by transiently suppressing blurred visual
inputs during rapid eye movements.
Finally, the present study focuses exclusively on visual responses during fixation periods, about
one to six seconds after a saccade, when perisaccadic modulations have subsided. As detailed
in the revised Methods (Line 596-603), all visual response trials evoked by grating motion that
occurred during periods of perisaccadic modulation were excluded to eliminate perisaccadic
effects. Therefore, the neuronal activity analyzed here reflects influences from factors like
glucose concentration changes over time, not from corollary discharge or other oculomotor-
related signals.
“In order to eliminate the influence of perisaccadic modulations on visual response analyses,
we first quantified the temporal extent of these modulations by aligning neuronal firing rates to
the onset and offset of saccades for each neuron. The duration of perisaccadic modulation was
determined using a standard-deviation-based criterion, identifying the time point where the
firing rate consistently returned to the stable baseline within a specified statistical tolerance. All
visual response data within these modulation time frames were excluded, thereby restricting
analyses to stable fixation periods and isolating them from perisaccadic modulations.”
Method
Were the animals only slightly sedated during recordings or deeply anaesthetized?
Authors: We appreciate you for raising this important point. In our study, animals were initially
anesthetized with ketamine (30 mg/kg) and dexmedetomidine (0.125 mg/kg) for surgical
preparation. The anesthetic depth was carefully monitored by respiration patterns and toe-pinch
reflexes. After surgery, animals were allowed several days to recover fully. On experimental
days, a light supplemental dose of ketamine (4 mg/kg) was administered solely for brief
handling. Recordings began at least 30-40 minutes later, when the animals were fully awake
and behaviorally recovered, consistent with established procedures (Azizpour & Hassani, 2012).
Thus, all neuronal recordings were conducted in awake, head-fixed birds under stable and
reproducible conditions.
As you suggested, we have clarified these details in the revised methods (Line: 383-411):
“Each animal was anesthetized by injecting ketamine (30 mg/kg) and dexmedetomidine (0.125
mg/kg) into the pectoral muscles. The anesthetic status was monitored by examining their
respiration patterns and reflex reactions to toe pinching (Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2017;
2008). Pigeons were wrapped with soft straps and positioned into a stereotaxic apparatus. After
a scalp incision, a lightweight steel head holder was affixed to the skull to ensure stable head
restraint in experiments. Guided by stereotaxic coordinates of the pigeon brain (Karten &
Hodos, 1967), recording windows over the left tectum, the left telencephalon, as well as a
pharmacological injection window over the cerebellum were surgically exposed by a dental
drill. The overlying dura mater remained intact. We also gently drilled a little fragment of the
orbital bone (1 × 1 mm) located on the top of the right eye, for the purpose of intraocular glucose
examinations and intraocular injections. After surgery, the scalp was sutured and prescribed
erythromycin ointment (BAIJINGYU Pharmaceutical, Nanjing, China). Pigeons were housed
individually and received Meloxicam (0.5 mg/kg, PO, once or twice daily) to alleviate
postoperative pain and ceftriaxone sodium (75 mg/kg, IM, every 6-8 hours) to prevent infection
for 3-7 days. Within 12-24 hours, their locomotion, feeding, and hydration behaviors had
resumed.
On experimental days, pigeons received a light dose of ketamine (4 mg/kg), were coated in a
soft bag, and situated on a foam couch. The head was secured to the stereotaxic apparatus via
the implanted head holder. Wound margins and surrounding muscles were periodically
infiltrated with lidocaine (Shanghaizhaohui Pharmaceutical, China). Experiments commenced
at least 30 min after light ketamine sedation when the animals had recovered, consistent with a
prior report (Azizpour & Hassani, 2012). All neuronal recordings were performed in awake,
head-fixed pigeons (Mahajan & Mysore, 2022; Neuenschwander et al., 1996; Xiao et al., 2024)
with unrestricted eye movements. During neuronal recordings, the left eye was covered while
the right eye was exposed to visual stimuli. For monitoring eye movements in the budgerigar,
chukar partridge, chicken and duck, animals underwent the same anesthesia and head-fixation
procedures. During the experiments, animals were not provided with food or water; however,
they had free access to both in their home cages before and after each session.
All procedures in this study were in strict accordance with the guidelines for the care and use
of animals established by the Society for Neuroscience. All of the animals were handled
according to protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Administration Committee at the
Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IBP-P-001(21) and IBP-P-001(24)).”
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary:
In this study, the authors investigated how oscillatory saccades (OS) modulate retinal glucose
dynamics and visual neuronal responses in awake, passively viewing pigeons. They monitored
eye movements and intraocular glucose levels, in some cases interstitial glucose, and also
recorded single-unit activity in three retinorecipient brain regions: the optic tectum (OT), the
nucleus opticus principalis thalami (nOPT), and the pretectal nucleus lentiformis mesencephali
(nLM) while birds viewed visual stimuli. Visual stimuli included naturalistic social videos of
pigeons, light/dark screen cycles, and large-field drifting gratings.
There are several key findings in the study. The authors demonstrate strong correlations
between visual stimulation and subsequent OS as well as between visual stimuli triggered OS
and subsequent increases in intraocular glucose levels and visual responses. Interestingly,
pharmacologically increasing retinal intraocular glucose via D-glucose injections enhanced
visual responses, while GluT-1 inhibition diminished these responses, causally linking
intraocular glucose levels to visual responses. Finally, suppressing OS via muscimol OS via muscimol injections
in the brainstem raphe complex diminished both intraocular glucose levels and visual responses,
thereby establishing a causal link from oscillatory saccades to visual responses through
modulation of intraocular glucose levels.
The strengths of this study are its rare combination of oculomotor, metabolic, and
neurophysiological measurements in awake birds, its well-controlled pharmacological
manipulations that establish causal links, and its demonstration that these effects occur across
multiple visual nuclei. However, while the causal role of oscillatory saccades in visual
processing is convincingly demonstrated, the attention-driven claims are unsupported by the
data. These should either be removed or require additional experiments to justify the link
between attention and oscillatory saccades.
Authors: We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful summary of our work and constructive
feedback. We appreciate the recognition of the strengths of our study, particularly the
integration of oculomotor, metabolic, and neurophysiological measurements in awake birds,
and the pharmacological manipulations that helped establish causal links between oscillatory
saccades, intraocular glucose dynamics, and visual neuronal responses.
We also fully understand and appreciate your concern regarding the attention-related
interpretation. In the revised manuscript, we have carefully revised our discussion to avoid
overstating this aspect. Specifically, we now describe saccades as stimulus-driven movements
that dynamically modulate retinal glucose supply and neuronal responsiveness, rather than
attributing them to attentional processes. We have removed all statements implying a link
between saccades and attention, and instead focus on their mechanistic role in coupling sensory-
driven eye dynamics with local metabolic regulation and neuronal activity.
Major Comments:
Specific conceptual critiques
1. Re: “which birds actively evoked saccades during attention-driven information gathering”
While here we have taken an example from a line from the abstract this is a recurring theme in
the manuscript and comes across as one of the major claims of the paper (which it should not
be). The evidence provided in the current manuscript does not demonstrate a direct (or indirect)
link between attention and OS and we disagree with the usage of this language in the manuscript,
including in the abstract, introduction and discussion.
Authors: Thank you so much for pointing out this important issue. Regarding the comment on
“attention”: we agree that our dataset in the prior submission does not directly measure
attentional states. We acknowledge that in the absence of explicit behavioral or task-based
measures of attention in our study, the initial phrasing in the prior submission could overstate
the evidence. We have corrected the related statements based on the ground truth, and now
emphasize the mechanistic role in linking visually driven eye movements to intraocular
metabolic regulation and neuronal responsiveness in the revised manuscript.
a) A ~3-4 min lag between oscillatory saccades (OSs) and response facilitation is incompatible
with moment-to-moment attentional modulation. These results are more consistent with a
“retinal readiness” hypothesis where scene changes trigger oscillatory saccades, elevating
retinal metabolic support for visual processing. the authors should reframe their interpretation
around metabolic maintenance rather than attention unless rapid, stimulus-locked effects are
demonstrated.
Authors: We greatly appreciate the insightful comment and agree that a ~3–4 min lag between
saccades and response facilitation is inconsistent with rapid, moment-to-moment attentional
modulation. In response, we have revised the manuscript to reframe our interpretation around
a mechanistic coupling between eye movement dynamics, local metabolic regulation, and
neuronal responsiveness, rather than attention. Specifically, we now characterize saccades as
visual stimulus-driven eye movements that modulate intraocular glucose levels and visual
neuronal activity, without inferring attentional involvement. We believe these revisions clarify
the scope of our conclusions and strengthen the mechanistic coherence and interpretive rigor of
the study.
b) Fig 1 j-n and Fig 1 o-s are strong evidence that it is changes in a visual scene that are
modulating oscillatory saccades rather than a more active and voluntary process as the authors
claim. Further, from Fig. 1 j-n, it seems to be just the presence of light (or a change from less
to more illumination) which might be driving increases in OS and subsequent glucose, visual
responses etc. In contrast a change from high luminance to dark as shown in Fig.1. o-s
diminishes OS. These pieces of evidence seem to suggest that this is a ‘reflexive’ mechanism
for priming the visual processing right from the retina which is the earliest node in the visual
processing hierarchy, rather than an active form of behavioral response, as claimed by the
authors.
Authors: Thank you again for this thoughtful and perceptive comment. As noted, Fig. 1j-s (now
updated as Fig. 1f-o) clearly demonstrate that changes in the visual scene, particularly
transitions between light and dark, strongly modulate both saccade frequency (Fig. 1g, l) and
oscillation frequency (Fig. 1h, m). These findings highlight a robust component of the
oculomotor response and support the view that saccades are triggered by visual scene changes.
Indeed, the enhancement of eye movements following illumination and their suppression in
darkness could suggest a reflexive mechanism that modulates visual processing, the earliest
stage in the visual hierarchy, by elevating local metabolic readiness. The visually driven
saccades observed during naturalistic social video viewing (Fig. 1p-r) further indicate that such
eye movements can be dynamically modulated under diverse visual conditions, extending
beyond simple luminance changes.
In the revised manuscript, we have accordingly reworded the Abstract, Results, and Discussion
to replace descriptions of saccades as “active” or “voluntary” with “stimulus-driven” or
“visually driven”, emphasizing their reflexive, stimulus-related nature. We believe these
revisions more accurately capture the underlying mechanism, align our interpretation with the
presented evidence, and strengthen the physiological coherence of the study.
c) The animal subjects in this study are passively viewing birds and are not actively behaving.
All experiments in this study have been conducted in passively viewing birds and not in
behaving birds performing a task. The authors use the terminology ‘ behaving birds’ at several
places in the manuscript (including methods) and these should be corrected using the
appropriate terminology in the field, for example ‘ passively viewing birds’, ‘ awake, head-
fixed’, etc (Neuenschwander et al, 1996, Mahajan and Mysore, 2022, Xiao et al, 2024).
Authors: We thank you for highlighting this important point. We agree that our experiments
were conducted in awake, head-fixed pigeons that were passively viewing visual stimuli, and
not in birds performing active behavior tasks. Our use of the phrase “behaving birds” was

the details of Fig. 2c–d. In the previous version, Fig. 2c–f presented data from an example
neuron recorded simultaneously with eye movements. Specifically, Fig. 2c and Fig. 2d depict

c) Fig. 2g. PCA - Do oscillation frequencies per saccade increase with saccade frequency?
If not, the way oscillation frequency is computed, a higher frequency could simply be a

Authors: Thank you so much for raising this insightful question regarding the relationship
between saccade frequency and oscillation frequency, as well as for the valuable suggestion to
conduct independent correlation analyses.
By combining your and other reviewers’ valuable suggestions, we have substantially revised
the manuscript to improve both conceptual clarity and methodological transparency.
Specifically, we introduced a new Figure 1 that systematically defines and contextualizes the
three behavioral metrics: saccade frequency, oscillation frequency, and intrasaccadic frequency,
within the established framework of avian saccadic eye movements. Saccade frequency was
defined as the number of saccades per analysis window. Oscillation frequency was the total
number of oscillatory cycles across all bursts within the window, reflecting the overall density
of oscillatory activity. Intrasaccadic frequency was the inverse of each oscillatory cycle’s
duration within a saccadic burst. This figure also illustrates how these parameters vary across
visual conditions (dark, light, gray screens and viewing social videos). The new analyses
demonstrate that only saccade frequency and oscillation frequency change significantly across
conditions, whereas intrasaccadic frequency remain stable, thereby providing a clearer
conceptual and quantitative foundation for subsequent neuronal and behavioral interpretations.
Although saccade and oscillation frequencies are overall positively correlated, their moment-
to-moment fluctuations are largely independent. Residual cross-correlation analyses confirmed
no evidence of noise-driven coupling, suggesting that they share a general trend but vary
independently in response to visual inputs. To clarify this relationship, we have included a new
plot in Figure 1e illustrating their correlation, which should help readers better interpret the
dynamics of avian saccadic eye movements.
Given the relationship between saccade and oscillation frequencies, we performed a principal
component analysis (PCA) to extract a unified component (PC1) capturing overall saccadic
activity strength. This approach could reduce collinearity between the two metrics and provided
a single, integrated variable for use in subsequent regression analyses. Nonetheless, we fully
agree that examining neuronal correlations with saccade frequency and oscillation frequency
separately provides complementary insight. Following this recommendation, we have now
included the new results in the revised supplementary figures (Supplementary Fig.6a-d).
Consistent with their shared partial correlation, the new results revealed distinct yet comparable
temporal structures, with both second- and minute-scale patterns evident in neuronal
correlations with saccade and oscillation frequencies. We believe these additions substantially
enhance the clarity, completeness, and analytical rigor of the manuscript, and we are grateful
for this constructive suggestion.
d) Fig. 2g - From the data, as mentioned earlier, it seems like the visual response enhancement

possibility that the observed enhancement in visual responses and increases in oscillation
frequency could reflect an early-session arousal or alertness effect, and we conducted additional
analyses to address this concern. The results indicate that such factors are unlikely to account
for the findings in Fig. 2g, for the following reasons.
First, the dataset comprised 127 neurons recorded from 37 individuals (on average 3-4 neurons
per animal). Before formal data collection, each neuron was tested using brief (300-ms)

corresponding neuronal responses were compared. If early-session arousal had contributed to

Other major comments
3. In Fig. 1i, why do the correlation coefficients increase in the pre-stimulus period? While
this is clear from the data in the example session shown in Fig. 1c, however, it seems that if
the effect is visible in the cumulative data in Fig. 1i, Fig. 1n and Fig. 1s, then this might
happen across sessions. Could this be due to an experimental artefact or due to predictability
in the 30 min stimulus transitions? It would be beneficial if the authors could give their
perspective on this.
Authors: Thank you for this insightful question. We agree that the pre-zero lag correlation
warrants careful examination and have performed additional analyses to address it. In our
opinion, the apparent rise in correlation coefficients before zero lag might be caused by the
intrinsic temporal structure of the signals being compared. The intraocular glucose fluctuation
varies smoothly over time and therefore exhibit strong autocorrelation. When such temporally
correlated signals are cross-correlated, the overlap between the slow, gradual changes in one
signal (e.g., glucose) and the faster changes in the other (e.g., saccade frequency or oscillation
frequency) can produce elevated correlation values at neighboring negative lags. In other words,
because the slow signal already shows an upward trend before the rapid change, partial
alignment occurs even when the lag is slightly negative. Therefore, the increase in correlation
coefficients before zero lag might reflect the autocorrelation and gradual trends of the signals,
rather than a causal influence of eye movements occurring before time zero. To address this,
we implemented a two-part analysis. First, we applied a modified cross-correlation analysis
using detrended and z-scored signals, with statistical significance assessed against a shuffle-
based null distribution. Second, to corroborate these findings with a method less susceptible to
autocorrelation, we applied an independent, standard-deviation (SD)-based threshold method
to estimate response latency. Reassuringly, both analyses yielded highly consistent results,
confirming that glucose responses lag behind saccade-related changes by approximately 3-4
minutes (Supplementary Fig. 3). We have updated the Methods section with a detailed
description of these approaches (Line 567-592).
4. The authors should include summary metrics for receptive field mapping and grating
orientation tuning data of recorded units in the supplementary material.
Authors: We appreciate your suggestion to include summary metrics for receptive field
mapping and grating orientation tuning. Although pigeons were head-fixed during
electrophysiological recordings, they were not trained to maintain visual fixation and freely
made saccades to orient their gaze. Therefore, it was not feasible to systematically map classical
receptive fields in the same way as in primate studies where gaze position can be precisely
controlled.
To assess visual responsiveness, we presented full-field square-wave gratings on a large screen
(130º × 140º) positioned 50 cm from the right eye, using an EPSON CB-535W projector. The
horizontal and vertical meridians of the grating field were rotated by 38° to match the pigeon’s
natural viewing geometry (Britto et al., 1990; Fu et al., 1998), following the same visual
stimulation protocol described in our previous studies of awake head-fixed pigeons. The
orientation of each grating was orthogonal to its direction of motion. Gratings were presented
for 300 ms, moving at 8°/s in one of four cardinal directions: temporal-to-nasal (T–N),
nasal-to-temporal (N–T), dorsal-to-ventral (D–V), or ventral-to-dorsal (V–D). For each neuron,
the direction of motion was customized to evoke the strongest visual response.
Although we did not perform precise receptive field mapping or restrict stimuli to localized
regions, the 300-ms large-field motion stimuli reliably evoked strong visual responses during
inter-saccadic periods. We agree that the quantifying direction tuning is fundamental for
understanding neuronal response properties. Accordingly, we have now included detailed
descriptions of the visual stimulation protocol in the Methods section and provided the
corresponding summary data in Supplementary Fig. 4, which add an overview of the tuning
properties of recorded units.
5. Line 243-244 - The authors should clarify what is meant by "...complexity of the
relationship between eye movements and visual processing", and what role does this
complexity serve? Similarly, in line 264 - “This short-term, second-scale modulation likely
served as an instant mechanism enabling…”. Why distinguish between second-scale and
minute-scale effects when the data suggests a monotonic increase in correlation? Does the
data support two mechanistically distinct processes?
Authors: We really appreciate your insightful question. By referring to the “complexity of the
relationship between eye movements and visual processing” we intended to highlight that
saccadic eye movements in birds influence visual responses across multiple temporal scales. At
the minute-scale, our data showed that saccades were followed by gradual increases in
intraocular glucose and enhanced neuronal responses, with a lag of ~3–4 minutes (Figs. 1, 2).
This effect likely reflects the cumulative impact of saccade-driven nutrient fluctuations over
minutes, supporting retinal responsiveness in the absence of retinal vasculature. At the second-
scale, neuronal responses increased transiently following individual saccades (Fig. 2g, i; Fig.
3), accompanied by spatially graded improvements in receptive fields near versus far from the
pecten (Fig. 3j–m). Inspired by reviewers’ comments, our additional analyses in the revised
manuscript further revealed that both saccade duration and the interval since the preceding
saccade correlated with visual response strength. Longer saccades likely induced stronger
mechanical agitation of intraocular fluid, whereas longer inter-saccade intervals allowed more
time for glucose diffusion to retinal cells (Supplementary Fig. 9). These findings support a rapid,
saccade-driven mechanism that transiently enhances nutrient delivery and visual
responsiveness.
Although the overall correlation profiles in Fig. 2 may appear monotonic, they encompass both
gradual, lagged effects over minutes and rapid, short-latency effects within seconds. We use the
terms “minute-scale” and “second-scale” to highlight these different temporal dynamics, which
likely reflect complementary aspects of the saccade-metabolism-response coupling in the avian
retina. Per your comment, we recognized that the term “complexity” was too general and
insufficiently specify. We have therefore replaced it with the phrase “multi-timescale coupling”,
to more accurately convey that avian saccades modulate visual processing through temporally
layered mechanisms, producing both immediate and cumulative effects that together optimize
retinal metabolic support and visual processing during natural viewing.
6. Would it be possible to compute the latency between the intraocular glucose peak and the
correlation peak (or the first instance of significant positive correlation) between OS and FR?
Authors: We greatly appreciate this insightful suggestion. In the study, saccades were recorded
simultaneously with either neuronal firing rates or continuous intraocular glucose (CGM),
but not both, as space limitations in the pigeon’s head precluded tri-modal recordings. During
pharmacological manipulations, intraocular glucose was monitored with a handheld glucometer,
enabling causal assessment of glucose changes but not continuous temporal alignment.
Therefore, a direct within-session latency between glucose peaks and saccade–FR correlations
cannot be computed.
To approximate temporal relationships across modalities, we implemented a cross-session
latency analysis aligned to saccade onset. (1) For saccade-glucose coupling (CGM sessions),
we computed lagged cross-correlations between saccade events and glucose signals and
identified the first time point exceeding a baseline threshold (mean ± 2.5 SD). (2) For saccade-
neuronal coupling (neurophysiology sessions), latency was defined as the delay corresponding
to the peak saccade-visual-response correlation (Fig. 2; Supplementary Figs. 6-8). (3) For
indirect glucose-visual-response coupling, we compared the mean latencies of these measures
under comparable behavioral conditions to approximate the glucose-neuron relationship. Both
analyses revealed consistent delays of about 3-4 minutes after changes in saccadic activity for
(1) alterations in intraocular glucose levels and (2) the peak of correlations between saccadic
activity and neuronal visual responses.
Applying these analyses to the muscimol experiments, we found that glucose changes lagged
behind reduced saccades by ~3-4 min (Fig. 5e), while neuronal suppression followed muscimol
injection by ~4.3 min, accounting for a 0.5-0.7 min pharmacological delay in saccade
suppression (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Thus, the effective delay between reduced saccades and
diminished neuronal responses was ~3.6-3.8 minutes, closely matching the saccade-glucose lag.
These results suggest that within roughly 3-4 minutes after saccades cease, both glucose supply
disruption and neuronal activity decline occur nearly simultaneously.
While this cross-session triangulation cannot replace a tri-modal simultaneous recording, the
convergent latencies strongly support the interpretation that saccade-driven metabolic
dynamics and neuronal responsiveness are temporally coupled on the minute scale. These
procedures and summary statistics have been added to the revised manuscript, and we note as
a priority for future work the development of a miniaturized tri-modal setup to obtain within-
animal, simultaneous latency estimates.

Authors: We appreciate the comment highlighting the need to clarify the methodology used to
estimate glucose levels. Pettigrew’s pioneering work in the tawny frogmouth demonstrated that
fluorescein dye can be rapidly propelled ~2–3 mm from the avian pecten within 2 seconds of a
single saccade, whereas during prolonged fixation dye diffusion was minimal (<0.5 mm even
after 120 s). This underscores the inefficiency of passive diffusion mechanisms and highlights
the essential role of saccades in nutrient delivery.
In our study, we aimed to approximate intraocular glucose dynamics in pigeons. Because
outward nutrient transport from the pecten involves a complex three-dimensional process of
diffusion, fluid motion, and metabolic consumption, we simplified the problem into a one-
dimensional diffusion model. In the revised Methods (Line 620-663), we have provided a full
description of this approach. Briefly, glucose dynamics in the vitreous were modeled according
to Fick’s second law, extended with a consumption term and a periodic mechanical component
representing saccadic oscillation. The model was parameterized using published values for
pigeon eye size, blood glucose concentrations, metabolic consumption rates, and diffusion
coefficients (Braun & Sweazea, 2008; Del Amo et al., 2017; Donovan, 1978; Koirala et al.,
2022; Von Eugen et al., 2022).
For simulation, we set the ocular radius to 7 mm (diameter ~13–14 mm) and considered two
retinal sites: a proximal site (1 mm from the pecten) and a distal site (4 mm from the pecten).
Physiological glucose concentrations were set to c1 = 15 mmol/L at the pecten and c2 = 13
mmol/L distally (Braun & Sweazea, 2008). The metabolic consumption rate was estimated from
pigeon brain tissue (27.29 ± 1.57 μmol/100 g/min ≈ 4.55×10−4 mmol/L/s(Von Eugen et al.,
2022), and the diffusion coefficient was derived from corrected water values at 40 °C, reduced
by half to approximate vitreous properties (≈ 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ mm²/s(Koirala et al., 2022)). A
periodic oscillatory term was included based on measured saccade intervals and amplitudes.
This model allowed us to generate time-dependent glucose concentration curves for proximal
and distal retinal locations, capturing the general trends of glucose diffusion influenced by
saccades. While these parameters cannot fully replicate the complex physicochemical
environment of the avian vitreous, the model provides a reasonable theoretical framework to
estimate how glucose availability differs across retinal regions (pecten-proximal vs. pecten-
distal). We also noted in the revised Methods that more precise modeling will require further
fluid-mechanics characterization of the avian vitreous.
Finally, are the other two nuclei, nOPT and nLM, topographically organized?
Authors: Thank you for raising this important point regarding the topographic organization of
the nOPT and nLM. In the case of the nOPT, as noted by Remy and Güntürkün (1991), the
retinal projections are relatively sparse, and retrograde tracing did not reveal a clear or
systematic retinotopic organization. This diffuse and weakly topographic projection pattern
prevents us from reliably inferring receptive field origins from electrode positions, unlike in the
OT where a robust retinotopic map exists. For the nLM, the situation differs somewhat.
Bodnarenko et al. (1988) demonstrated the presence of a retinotopic map in this nucleus.
However, the retinal ganglion cells projecting to the nLM are concentrated in a horizontal band
near the retinal equator, while input from central visual field regions is sparse. These precludes
reliable group comparisons of proximal versus distal representations analogous to those we
conducted in the OT. Taken together, while both nOPT and nLM play important roles in avian
visual processing, the specific anatomical and projection features of OT make it more amenable
to the type of spatially structured analyses we pursued here.

whether muscimol injection into the Raphe complex affects glucose release from the pecten,
independent of saccades, is highly relevant.
First, to our knowledge, muscimol in the Raphe complex, a GABA receptor agonist, does not
A
directly alter glucose transporter activity in the pecten. Our data indicate that its principal effect
is to abolish normal saccadic eye movements (Fig. 5b and c), accompanied by a significant
decrease in intraocular glucose levels, from 16.00 ± 2.01 to 11.45 ± 2.08 mmol/L (p < 0.001;
normalized data in Fig. 5d).
Second, if glucose delivery were driven effectively by passive diffusion from the pecten,
one would indeed expect delayed, weaker correlations to persist. However, classic work by
Pettigrew et al. (1990) demonstrated that fluorescein dye can be actively propelled 2–3 mm
from the avian pecten within ~2 s following a saccade, whereas diffusion during fixation
remains minimal (<0.5 mm even after 120 s). This observation indicates that passive diffusion
alone cannot effectively transport nutrients within the retina.
Third, additional analyses of the muscimol data provided further supporting evidence. We
appreciate your suggestion to include correlation analyses similar to Fig. 2g. However, due to
spatial constraints in the pigeons’ heads, it was not feasible to record saccades, neuronal firing,
and intraocular glucose continuously and simultaneously within the same sessions, which
precluded meaningful correlation analyses with firing rates. Nevertheless, we performed
complementary analyses showing that saccadic eye movements and neuronal visual responses
were significantly reduced within 0.5-0.7 min (Fig. 5f; Supplementary Fig. 3f) and ~4.3 min (p
< 0.001) after muscimol injection, respectively. This ~3-4-minute lag between the reduction in
saccade frequency and the onset of neuronal inhibition closely matched the 3–4-minute delay
between muscimol-induced suppression of saccades and the subsequent decline in intraocular
glucose (Fig. 5e). Together, these results further support the interpretation that disrupting the
saccade-driven pumping mechanism impairs glucose distribution and visual function.
To clarify these points, we have reorganized and revised text accordingly. We also corrected
Fig. 5g by labeling trial numbers for both before and muscimol conditions, making it clear that
neuronal visual responses decreased progressively following muscimol injection.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
Oscillatory saccades are high frequency (~10-40 Hz) eye movements that often accompany
translational eye saccades in birds. Xu et al. hypothesize that (1) oscillatory saccades are
initiated during visual behaviors that require higher nutrient levels in the retina; (2) these
saccades distribute nutrients (specifically glucose) in the eye, and (3) this increased glucose
distribution improves retinal processing of images.
In support of (1), they show an immediate increase in saccade frequency and oscillation
frequency (although these terms require clarification) upon salient changes in visual input. In
support of (2), they find that intraocular glucose concentrations increase ~3 minutes later and
demonstrate causality by pharmacologically supressing saccades. In support of (3), they record
increased neural responses to visual stimuli in retino-recipient nuclei also ~3 min after periods
of increased saccades. They again provide some evidence for causality through intraocular
glucose injections which increase neural responses, and suppression of saccades which decrease
neural responses.
The neural data, intraocular glucose recording, and simultaneous causal manipulations are
technically challenging and are of particular interest. The main issues revolve around better
contextualizing the specific role of oscillatory saccades, and improving the analysis and
interpretation of temporal correlations between saccades, glucose concentrations, and neural
activity. Overall, the authors provide convincing evidence for a link between oscillatory
saccades, glucose distribution, and visual processing. The result is a fascinating example of
how a neural system solves a challenging metabolic problem, and should therefore be of broad
interest.

Authors: Thank you so much for raising this critical point and for suggesting the inspiring
reference (Harris, 2021). We fully agree that, given slow temporal dynamics, it is essential to
rule out “nonsense correlations” arising from sample non-independence and shared drifts.
Following the suggestion, we implemented two shuffling-based control analyses to statistically
validate the temporal coupling between saccadic and neuronal measures.
First, we employed the Pseudosession Method, which tests whether the observed correlations
are genuinely locked to stimulus timing or could emerge from chance alignments of slow
fluctuations in eye movements and neuronal firing. For each neuron, we generated a surrogate
time series of stimulus onsets by randomly shuffling the inter-trial intervals (ITIs) from the
original session, thereby preserving the ITI distribution while disrupting the true temporal
alignment between saccadic history and visual stimuli. As shown in the left panel of
Supplementary Fig. 7, the mean correlation coefficients from the real data (orange line)
systematically deviated from the null distribution (gray shaded area) obtained from the shuffled
event times, indicating that the correlations were specifically time-locked to the actual visual
stimuli.
Second, we applied the Session Permutation Method, which assesses whether the correlations
are specific to matched neuronal and saccadic metrics from the same recording session, rather
than reflecting shared slow drifts across sessions or animals. Each neuron’s recording (n = 54)
was treated as an independent session. We generated a null distribution by pairing the visual-
response time series from one neuron with the saccadic-metric series from a different, randomly
selected neuron. As shown in the right panel of Supplementary Fig. 7, the mean correlation
coefficients from the true pairings diverged from those in the shuffled dataset. Notably,
significant negative correlations were observed at the second-scale and significant positive
correlations at the minute-scale, confirming that the temporal relationships we observed are not
artifacts of overlapping saccade histories or slow session-level drifts.
We have incorporated these two shuffling-based control analyses into the revised manuscript,
which we believe provide additional support for our findings.

oscillatory saccades and neural response doesn't make sense.
- The authors imply that both the positive correlation at ~3-4 minute timescale and the negative
correlation at <6 s timescale are due to slow dynamics of glucose diffusion from the pectin oculi
to retinal ganglion cells. However, these timescales differ by over an order of magnitude.
Which is it? Does it takes seconds or minutes for glucose to diffuse and increase neural firing
rates?
Authors: Thank you so much for this important comment. We have clarified the distinction
between the two timescales in the revised manuscript.
The second-scale negative correlation (< 6 s) is directly supported by both the neuronal
response data and our biophysical simulation (Fig. 3). Neuronal visual responses increased
progressively with longer stimulus-saccade intervals after each saccade (Fig. 3). Additional
analyses of the latest saccade duration further revealed that the longer saccades significantly
enhanced subsequent neuronal visual responses, as your following comments suggested (see
details later). These findings support a local convective–diffusive relaxation process triggered
by fluid perturbations induced by a single saccade. Consistent with this interpretation, our
simulation based on Fick’s second law predicted that intraocular glucose concentration re-
equilibrates within a few seconds over inner-retinal distances, matching the timescale of the
observed neuronal response dynamics. Thus, the second-scale modulation likely reflects a brief
adjustment of nutrient gradients following eye motion.
In contrast, the minute-scale positive correlation (~3-4 min) represents a slow cumulative effect
in which saccades, through fluid-dynamic agitation, enhance glucose diffusion relative to its
metabolic consumption, gradually improving nutrient availability in the avascular avian retina.
Repetitive saccadic eye movements increase the effective diffusivity of glucose and promote
mild convection, producing a slowly accumulating imbalance between metabolic consumptions
and nutrient delivery, and consequently a gradual rise in intraocular glucose concentration. This
long-term process aligns closely with the delayed enhancement of intraocular glucose levels
and neuronal responsiveness observed in the study.
Together, these findings support a dual-timescale mechanism: a rapid convective–diffusive
recovery that occurs within seconds after each saccade, and a slow cumulative enhancement of
metabolic support that builds up over minutes through repeated saccades. We have now clarified
that the slow correlation most likely reflects a cumulative metabolic process, whereas the fast
correlation reflects a transient, mechanically induced modulation, indicating that distinct
mechanisms rather than a single diffusion process spanning both timescales.
Are there alternate explanations for the short + long time scale effects? E.g. since responses are
measured downstream in retino-recipient areas, could post-saccadic suppression play a role?
Could mechanical disturbance affect RGC firing?
Authors: Thank you for this insightful comment. We fully agree that post-saccadic modulation
represents a critical mechanism that can influence neuronal activity following saccades. Indeed,
our earlier study (Yan Yang et al., 2008) demonstrated robust peri-saccadic modulation in the
pigeon visual system, including transient suppression during saccades followed by a post-
saccadic facilitation phase (Fig. R6, adapted from Yan Yang et al. (2008)). In that work,
neuronal activity in both the nucleus opticus principalis thalami (nOPT) and nucleus lentiformis
mesencephali (nLM) exhibited a characteristic pattern of pre-saccadic inhibition followed by
post-saccadic enhancement lasting serval hundred milliseconds. This temporal profile contrasts
sharply with the present findings, in which neuronal visual responses exhibited gradual, multi-
second modulations following the latest saccade onset.
Figure R6 Perisaccadic modulation in visual neurons in pigeons (Yan Yang et al., 2008).
Notably, to minimize potential contamination from peri-saccadic modulations, we implemented
exclusion criteria in the present analyses. As detailed in the Methods, we first quantified the
duration of peri-saccadic modulations by aligning neuronal firing rates to both the onset and
offset of saccades. This duration was objectively determined using an SD-based criterion,
identifying the time point at which firing rate consistently returned to baseline stability. All
visual response data failing within these modulation windows were subsequently excluded,
ensuring that the analysis focused exclusively on stable fixation periods. Visual response to the
300-ms grating probe were calculated by subtracting a baseline defined as the mean
spontaneous firing rate during a 300-ms window aligned to the probe timing relative to the
preceding saccade. Thus, we are confident that the second-scale effects analyzed in this study,
such as the gradual increase process lasting up to ~6 s (Fig. 3), extend well beyond the temporal
range of the classic, sub-second peri-saccadic modulations.
Regarding the possibility that mechanical perturbations of the eye might influence retinal
ganglion cell (RGC) activity, we agree that this is an important consideration. Prior work
(Marrese et al., 2019) showed that sustained mechanical indentation ( 10 μm displacement for
60 second) can modulate RGC firing rates. Although saccades in our dataset last only a few
∼
hundred milliseconds, and all data during saccades were excluded from the analysis, we
acknowledge that subtle mechanical effects cannot be entirely ruled out. We have added this
point to the Discussion to provide a more comprehensive and balanced interpretation of the
results.
Or, are there behavioral correlations that could explain this short timescale effect? E.g. are birds
particularly likely to make a saccade when glucose is already quite low, or are saccades
regularly spaced in time? A more complete description of saccade statistics would likely help

If the mechanism is totally unknown, that is fine, but the discussion should be more transparent.
Authors: We thank you for these constructive suggestions. We agree that potential behavioral
correlates of the short timescale effects warrant careful examination. To address this, we
analyzed the temporal statistics of saccades. Our data show that saccades were not regularly
spaced in time but instead occurred with variable inter-saccade intervals, following a right-
skewed distribution (mean ± SD: 2.73 ± 1.93 s; Fig. R7). Moreover, bidirectional manipulations
of intraocular glucose levels robustly modulated visual responses, but did not alter saccadic eye
movements, indicating that the observed short-timescale modulation of visual activity is
unlikely to arise from regular saccade timing or preferential saccades triggered under low-
glucose conditions.

inter-saccade intervals across animals. The dashed line indicates the 95% distribution interval.
Regarding the possibility that mechanical agitation enhances both glucose uptake and diffusion
across multiple timescales, direct physiological evidence is currently lacking. Nevertheless, this
mechanism aligns well with the coexistence of both second- and minute-scale correlations
observed in our data. Specifically, transient mechanical agitation during individual saccades
could rapidly promote glucose diffusion and utilization that facilitate neuronal responses over
a few seconds, whereas cumulative increases in saccadic eye movements could gradually create
imbalance between metabolic consumption and nutrient delivery, leading to a gradual rise in
intraocular glucose concentration over minutes. We have revised the Discussion to clarify this
interpretation and to explicitly acknowledge the uncertainty surrounding the precise underlying
mechanism. We appreciate your emphasis on transparency and have expanded the revised text
to distinguish established physiological observations from more speculative hypotheses.

Authors: Thank you very much for highlighting the potential role of oxygen diffusion. While
our study primarily measured glucose dynamics, we agree that other nutrients, particularly
oxygen, could contribute to the functional role of saccades. Oxygen diffusion and blood flow
are indeed essential for retinal metabolism. Wingstrand et al. reported the crucial role of the

pigeons, they observed an oxygen partial pressure gradient from the pecten to the retinal
periphery, and vessel occlusion caused a sharp drop in oxygen tension accompanied by retinal
degeneration. Wallman et al. further proposed that saccadic oscillations may facilitate the
diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the avian pecten to the retina. However, direct
experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis remains limited.
In the present study, we directly monitored intraocular glucose dynamics using a continuous
glucose monitoring (CGM) system and found a temporal correlation between glucose
fluctuations and saccade activity. We have now added a statement in the Discussion
acknowledging that oxygen (and potentially other metabolic substrates) may also play a role
and that differences in their diffusion and transport properties could modulate their
physiological relevance. We explicitly state that our conclusions are based on glucose-
dependent evidence and do not exclude possible contributions from oxygen or other nutrients.
Future work may test whether saccades similarly modulate intraocular oxygen levels and visual
sensitivity.

Authors: We sincerely thank you for this valuable suggestion, which has helped us improve
both the precision and the mechanistic clarity of the revised manuscript.
Following the direct D-glucose injection, our analysis showed that the enhancement of neuronal
responses was very rapid, with a latency of only 0.25 minutes (15 seconds, p < 0.05).
Conversely, inhibiting glucose transport with Bay-876 resulted in a decrease in neuronal
responses with a latency of 1.25 minutes (p < 0.05). These findings confirm that neuronal
activity is indeed highly sensitive to local glucose availability. We have clarified the
methodology for this analysis in the revised Methods section:
"To assess post-injection dynamics of neuronal activity, data were aligned to the injection time
and analyzed in 0.5-min windows. Activity in each window was z-score normalized to the pre-
injection baseline (outliers >3 standardized MAD excluded). The latency of significant change
was defined as the median time of the first window differing from baseline."
Regarding the Raphe complex inhibition experiment, our data demonstrate a 3-4 minute lag
from the reduction in saccadic metrics to the decline in intraocular glucose concentrations (Fig.
5e) . To address the specific question about the lag with the neuronal response, our new analyses
revealed a consistent delay of about 4.3 minutes from the muscimol injection to the attenuation
of neuronal responses. Crucially, we also determined there was a 0.5-0.7 min delay between the
injection and the actual suppression of eye movements (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Therefore,
when accounting for this initial pharmacological delay on eye movements, the resulting lag
between the cessation of saccades and the subsequent decline in neuronal responses is
approximately 3.6-3.8 minutes. The close correspondence between these two key time lags: the
3.6–3.8-minute delay from reduced saccades to neuronal responses inhibition and the 3-4-
minute delay from reduced saccades to decreased intraocular glucose concentrations (Fig. 5e),
suggest that within approximately 3-4 minutes after saccades cease, both glucose supply
disruption and neuronal activity decline occur nearly simultaneously.

Authors: Thank you so much for the valuable comment. We apologize that the original wording
(“sustained” and “precise shaping”) was misleading and did not accurately reflect our results.
We do not distinguish between sustained and transient neuronal responses, nor do we provide
evidence for receptive-field sharpening. Our findings instead show that avian saccades are
closely coupled with fluctuations in intraocular glucose levels, suggesting a mechanism that
helps maintain retinal energy availability during visual processing. Accordingly, we have
revised the statement to read more conservatively, noting that saccades may support retinal

Authors: We fully understand your concerns and appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point.
First, in pigeons, all saccades are inherently oscillatory(Wallman & Letelier, 1993). The
oscillatory component is an intrinsic feature of each saccade rather than a distinct type of eye
movement. Each saccadic eye movement therefore combines a positional shift with embedded
high-frequency (~30Hz) oscillations in pigeons (Nye, 1969). As in mammals, one function of
a saccade in birds is to reorient gaze toward a new location of interest. We apologize that the
term “oscillatory saccades” in the previous version may have been misleading. In the revised
manuscript, we have clarified three properties of avian saccades in Figure 1. Among them, the
~30 Hz oscillatory frequency itself, as correctly note, is too fast to serve a visual scanning or
gaze orientation, which are accomplished by the overall saccadic displacement.
Second, during saccade, visual input is likely blurred, akin to viewing a scene through a rapidly
shaking camera. However, these blurred images are not normally processed by the brain
because of saccadic visual suppression. Previous studies have demonstrated that, in pigeons,
activity along the primary visual pathways, from the nOPT to higher visual centers, is strongly
suppressed during saccades by corollary discharge signals from the Raphe complex (Yan Yang
et al., 2008), paralleling the phenomenon of saccadic suppression in humans that prevents
perception of motion blur during rapid eye movements.
Taken together, these observations suggest that saccadic eye movements in pigeons may serve
dual roles: beyond their gaze orienting function, they may also contribute to maintaining retinal
health and metabolic homeostasis through movement-coupled perfusion and nutrient-delivery
mechanisms. We have revised the corresponding text to clarify these distinctions and to better
articulate the broader physiological implications.

Authors: We appreciate your insightful feedback on the definition and interpretation of our
behavioral metrics. As noted, “saccade frequency” (or rates of saccades) and “oscillation
frequency” are central to our study but were not clearly defined in the original submission.
Saccades are rapid, oscillatory bursts of eye movements at periodic intervals in pigeons (Nye,
1969; Wallman & Letelier, 1993). To capture their temporal organization, we included a
detailed definition in the revised manuscript: 1) Saccade frequency: the number of detected
saccades per analysis window, representing the rate of oscillatory episodes occurred. 2)
Oscillation frequency: the total number of oscillatory cycles embedded within all saccades in
an analysis window, representing the overall temporal density of oscillatory activity. 3)
Intrasaccadic frequency: the reciprocal of each oscillatory cycle duration, reflecting the
oscillation rate within a saccadic burst (typically 20–30 Hz in our data, consistent with Nye
(1969). The revised Fig. 1c now systematically illustrated theses three frequency-related
metrics, saccade frequency (F ), oscillation frequency (F ), and intrasaccadic frequency
sac osci
(F ) along with their relation to the established characteristics of avian saccadic eye

movements in the literature. The updated figure also shows how these metrics vary across
different visual conditions in pigeons (Fig. 1d, e). These new results demonstrate that only
saccade frequency and oscillation frequency changed significantly across viewing conditions,
thereby providing a clearer foundation for subsequent analyses and interpretation.
Regarding the lower baseline frequencies, the higher “oscillation frequencies” (~20-30 hz)
reported in the earlier studies correspond to intrasaccadic frequency, not to the oscillation
frequency as defined in this study. Our intrasaccadic frequency (20–30 Hz) is fully consistent

time window. Frequencies were calculated using a moving-window approach, in which a 1-
minute window was slid across the entire experimental timeline in 0.1-minute (6-second) steps,

7. Fig. 3j - What is the model?
Authors: Thank you for your question concerning the model, which is important in the study.
The model implanted in Fig. 3j is a conceptual diffusion-consumption framework designed to
simulate intraocular glucose concentration dynamics under the influence of saccades. We
adopted this simplified approach to estimate how saccadic oscillations might modulate glucose
accessibility at different retinal loci.
A full description of the model is now included in the revised Methods (Lines 620–663). The
model is based on Fick’s second law of diffusion, extended to include a glucose consumption
term and a periodic mechanical perturbation term to represent saccadic effects. Anatomical and
physiological parameters (e.g. ocular radius, baseline glucose concentrations, metabolic
consumption rates, and diffusion coefficients; (Braun & Sweazea, 2008; Del Amo et al., 2017;
Donovan, 1978; Koirala et al., 2022; Von Eugen et al., 2022)) were drawn from published data
or experimentally measured values. Two retinal distances were modeled: one proximal (~1 mm
from the pecten) and one more distal (~4 mm from the pecten). The simulation yields time-
dependent glucose concentration curves at each location, illustrating the relative effect of
saccadic activity on nutrient distribution and spatial gradients. While the model does not capture
the full complexity of three-dimensional vitreous fluid flow and biochemical interactions, it
provides a quantitative framework for comparing glucose dynamics between regions and
assessing the potential contribution of saccadic eye movements to nutrient delivery. We have
updated the legend of Fig. 3 and added a detailed description in the Methods to clarify the
model’s construction and underlying assumptions, which we believe will enhance clarity and
interpretability for readers.
8. Fig. 4c - What is the color scale? How can neurons have a response of -30 sp/s? Also please
add start & ending trial numbers.
Authors: The color scale in Fig. 4C represents baseline-corrected neuronal firing rates (spikes/s).
In this study, a 300-ms grating motion served as a probe to assess neuronal visual responses,
and firing rates were computed in 50-ms bins. Baselines were defined as average spontaneous
firing rates during saccade intervals without probes, aligned to the time point of prior probe.
Visual responses to the grating motion were obtained by subtracting this baseline from the
probe-evoked firing rate. Accordingly, negative values indicate suppression below baseline
firing, whereas positive values indicate excitatory responses to the grating motion. In
accordance with your suggestion, we have added annotations for the starting and ending trial
(probe) numbers in the revised figure.
9. Line 171 - What does "A 5.00-6.00" refer to?
Authors: Thank you for raising this point. "A 5.00–6.00" refers to stereotaxic coordinates of the
pigeon brain. Our coordinate system follows the standards established by Karten and Hodos
(1967), which remains the reference for avian brain anatomy. Here, "A" stands for anterior,
indicating a position along the anterior–posterior axis relative to the reference point (bregma).
The values 5.00–6.00 denote the distance in millimeters (mm) from bregma. In avian
neuroanatomy, bregma (the intersection of the sagittal suture and the mid-plane of the ear canals)
is conventionally used as the origin for stereotaxic coordinates, from which anterior (A),
posterior (P), dorsal (D), ventral (V), medial (M), and lateral (L) directions are defined. We
apologize for the lack of explicit unit labeling in the manuscript. In the revision, we have added
“mm” when these coordinates first appear, included a brief explanation of the notation, and
cited the stereotaxic atlas for clarity.

and oscillatory saccades? It is unclear if effects are due to suppression of the oscillatory
component specifically.
Authors: We appreciate for the important question. In pigeons, each saccade comprises of a
burst of oscillatory cycles. The Raphe complex is critical for generating the oscillatory
component. Muscimol injections into the Raphe complex selectively suppressed the oscillatory
activity. Thus, Raphe complex inactivation does specifically disrupt oscillatory dynamics,
supported by our previous lesion studies (Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang Yang et al., 2008). We
have clarified this point in the revised manuscript.
11. Discussion - Studies have demonstrated dramatic differences in eye movements in head
fixed vs. unrestrained birds. See Land 2015 and Gioanni 1988. Are oscillations equally
important when the head is free to move? Have they been demonstrated in both head fixation
and free motion?
Authors: We appreciate you for raising this important point and for highlighting the relevant
references. Eye movements during optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) can indeed differ between
head-fixed and unrestrained conditions, especially in the gain relationship between the slow
phase of OKN and the stimulus velocity. Nevertheless, the oscillatory component of saccades
has been shown to be a robust and consistent feature across behavioral conditions. Multiple
studies employing high-temporal resolution methods, including search coil system and EOG
recordings, have demonstrated that oscillations occur during both spontaneous saccades and the
quick phases of OKN in head-free as well as head-fixed birds (Gioanni, 1988; Land, 2015;
Wallman & Letelier, 1993; Xiao et al., 2023; Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang Yang et al., 2008). To
further illustrate this point, we have added a supplementary video (Supplementary Video 6)
showing saccades with oscillatory components in a head-free pigeon, observed both when the
head was still and when it was moving. We also compared stimulus-driven saccades during
viewing of light, dark, and gray screens, as well as during presentation of social mating videos
(updated Fig. 1). In the present study, head fixation was applied to ensure stable recordings of
well-isolated single-neuron activity. These methodological considerations have been clarified
in the revised Methods section.
12. Line 274 - Reference 50 doesn't contain any mention of the Raphe complex. It would be
helpful to clarify the proposed role of the Raphe complex in generation of regular saccades vs.
oscillatory saccades.
Authors: We thank you for the careful observation. You are correct that Reference 50 does not
explicitly mention the raphe complex. Instead, it provides a broad review of brainstem
mechanisms underlying saccade control, particularly the role of omnipause neurons (OPNs).
The Raphe complex, especially the nucleus raphe interpositus (RIP), contains OPNs that fire
tonically during fixation but pause during saccades in all directions, thereby gating saccade.
In birds, virtually all saccades contain oscillatory components (Wallman & Letelier, 1993),
even when the head is free to move (see new Supplementary Video 6). Our previous lesion studies
have shown that disruption of the Raphe complex eliminate saccadic oscillations dramatically
(Yan Yang et al., 2008). Thus, the Raphe complex plays a key role in generating avian saccades.
In light of this clarification, we have removed the original citation and revised the text to clearly
describe the specific features of avian saccades and the role of the Raphe complex.
13. Line 321-322. I believe the authors mean "intraocular", not "interocular".
Authors: Thank you so much for catching this mistake. We have corrected interocular to
intraocular in the revised manuscript.
14. Methods: How many individuals of the non-pigeon species were used? Were the surgical
procedures the same for these animals (the methods refer to pigeons when describing most
procedures)?
Authors: We thank you for this important question regarding animal use and procedures. As
shown in Figure 1, we included four additional bird species besides pigeons, with one individual
from each species. Eye movements in these birds were recorded using electrooculography
(EOG), following the same surgical and recording procedures described for pigeons. Among
them, only one chukar partridge was euthanized for eyeball collection after the procedure
(Supplementary Fig. 1c). All animals were housed and cared for in accordance with institutional
animal care guidelines and approved protocols, and with full consideration for animal welfare.
15. Methods, "Visual conditions" - How many 30 or 60 min visual presentations were delivered
in a single session? Were animals given food and water during sessions?
Authors: Thanks for this question. In the video presentation experiments, pigeons were exposed
to a gray screen for 30-40 minutes, followed by a 30-minute presentation of mating videos (Fig.
1p in the revised version). For the light/dark stimulation experiments, the screens alternated
between white (RGB: 255, 255, 255) and black (RGB: 0, 0, 0) at 60-minute intervals (Fig. 1f,
k in the revised version). Each behavioral session lasted approximately 3-4 hours. Animals were
not provided with food or water during the sessions but had free access to both before and after
the experiments when in their home cages. We have added these details to the Methods section.
16. Line 480 - "saccades" – typo
Authors: Thank you for catching this typo. We have corrected the sentence in the revised
manuscript.
17. Figures are very low resolution
Authors: We thank you for pointing this out. All figures have been updated with high-resolution
versions to improve clarity and readability. We believe these revisions will help readers better
discern the details of the data presentation.

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This

provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have properly responded to my questions. This is a fine paper now.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have provided all requested clarifications and addressed all of our questions from the previous round of review.
The adjustment of how the findings were framed, methodological clarifications, addition of support analyses, and
improvements to figures and descriptions have strengthened the authors’ work.
Major Comments:
Figure 1d:
1. While the one-way ANOVA shows a significant effect, it does not indicate which of the L, D, V, and G groups differ
pairwise—only that at least one pair differs. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons (such as Tukey's HSD or corrections for multiple
comparisons) are needed to identify which specific conditions differ.
2. Additionally, ~770 time windows are treated as independent observations (df = 771, 768), but these are repeated
measurements from continuous recordings within the same pigeons. Time windows from the same animal and the same
recording are not independent. They share individual-level variance and are temporally correlated. We suggest using a
repeated-measures ANOVA, or a linear mixed-effects model with pigeon identity as a random effect to properly account for
non-independence, where possible.
Overall, the study is technically impressive and will be of broad interest. We do not need to review the revised manuscript
again, provided that the Nature Communications editorial team ensures that the authors include the required methodological
details. Once the comments shared in this round are incorporated, the manuscript will be ready for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have thoroughly addressed my main concerns with the original manuscript. My only remaining comment is
regarding my original major point 2: Thank you for including this more systematic analysis of the temporal relationship
between neural activity and saccade frequency. The analysis is quite helpful, but I am concerned by the diagonal structure in
Supplementary Fig 8. Are the authors sure that this is not an artifact of how the sliding windows are centered in the analysis?
It seems odd that the optimal time lag should shift so systematically with the window width. It is possible that a
methodological issue is obscuring a more consistent result across window widths, compatible with the ~3 min delays
reported elsewhere in the paper. (There is also an issue with the tick marks in FigS8e, right panel.) I urge them to take a
look, but overall recommend the article for publication.

Authors: We appreciate the time and effort you dedicated to reviewing our work. Your
constructive comments in the previous round have substantially improved the quality of this
manuscript.
Authors: We sincerely thank you for the favorable assessment of our revised manuscript and
for the helpful recommendations regarding the statistical methodology of Fig. 1d. We fully
agree that 1) post-hoc tests are needed to identify which conditions differ after a significant
omnibus ANOVA, and 2) treating time windows as independent observations can inflate the
degrees of freedom because repeated measurements from the same pigeon are not independent.
Per your suggestions, we have added multiple-comparison-corrected post-hoc pairwise
comparisons and re-analysed the data using a linear mixed-effects model (LMM), with pigeon
identity included as a random effect to account for repeated measurements.
1) Post-hoc pairwise comparisons following the one-way ANOVA
As you noted, a one-way ANOVA indicates that at least one group differs but does not identify
which pairs of conditions differ (Light, Dark, Video, and Gray). We therefore have added
Tukey’s HSD post-hoc tests following each ANOVA to perform pairwise comparisons with
appropriate control for multiple testing.
i. Saccade frequency (Fig. R1a): the dark condition was significantly lower than the light,
video, and gray conditions (all p < 0.001). Additionally, light was higher than gray (p =
0.02), and video was higher than the gray condition (p < 0.001).
ii. Oscillation frequency (Fig. R1b): the dark condition was significantly lower than the
video condition (p < 0.001), and the video condition was significantly higher than the
gray condition (p < 0.001).
iii. Intrasaccadic frequency (Fig. R1c): no significant pairwise differences were observed
among conditions (all Tukey-adjusted p > 0.05).
Fig. R1 | Pairwise comparisons of eye movement metrics across visual conditions.
a-c, Pairwise comparison matrices for saccade frequency (a), oscillation frequency (b), and
intrasaccadic frequency (c) derived from one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD post-hoc
tests. d-f, Pairwise comparison matrices for the same metrics derived from a linear mixed-
effects model followed by Wald tests, with Pigeon ID included as a random effect to account
for repeated measurements. Colors and numbers indicate the significance level (p values) of
differences between conditions (Dark, Light, Gray, and Video). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p
< 0.001.
2) Accounting for non-independence across time windows (repeated measurements)
We agree with you that, in the previous version, the non-overlapping 1-minute time windows
sampled from the same pigeons were not independent. To address this, we re-analyzed each
saccade metric using a linear mixed-effects model, with “Condition” as a fixed effect and
“Pigeon ID” as a random intercept: Frequency ~ Condition + (1 | Pigeon ID). This approach
accounts for between-subject variability and avoids inflating degrees of freedom due to within-
subject repeated sampling. We also conducted post-hoc pairwise comparisons within the LMM
framework (estimated marginal means with Wald tests and multiple-comparison correction).
The LMM results confirm and strengthen our conclusions.:
i. Saccade frequency (Fig. R1d): The fixed effect of condition remained highly significant,
F(3, 771) = 52.29, p < 0.001. Post-hoc tests indicated significant differences for most
condition pairs, except light vs. video.
ii. Oscillation frequency (Fig. R1e): The fixed effect of condition was also significant, F(3,
768) = 16.63, p < 0.001. Post-hoc tests showed significant differences for most pairs,
except gray vs. dark and gray vs. light.
iii. Intrasaccadic frequency (Fig. R1f): no effect of condition was observed (F(3, 765) =
0.29, p = 0.83), and no significant pairwise differences were detected.
We have updated the manuscript to include these additional statistical procedures in detail and
added a new supplementary figure (Supplementary Fig. 2) summarizing the full pairwise
comparison matrices for both the ANOVA with Tukey’s HSD and the LMM-based post-hoc
tests (Wald tests).
Authors: Thank you so much for your careful reading and the positive assessment of the
revision. We also appreciate for raising this important methodological question regarding the
diagonal structure in the supplementary Fig. 8 (now updated as Supplementary Fig. 9).
To assess whether the apparent systematic shift in optimal lag with window width could be an
artifact of how the sliding windows are referenced/centered, we re-ran the analysis using
alternative definitions of the time lag. Specifically, we defined the lag relative to (i) the end of
the window (trailing-edge; Supplementary Fig. 9), (ii) the midpoint of the window (centered,
Fig. R2a, c, e), and (iii) the onset of the window (leading-edge, Fig. R2b, d, f). Across all three
definitions, the resulting correlation maps were qualitatively similar and consistently exhibited
a clear diagonal ridge (Fig. R2a-f), indicating that the structure is not driven by window
centering/alignment choices or by the particular reference point used to define the lag.
We therefore interpret the diagonal feature as a consequence of evaluating correlations across
combinations of window widths and lags when the relationship is dominated by eye-movement
activity within a relatively fixed, minute-scale pre-stimulus interval (~3 min). Under this
scenario, elevated correlations arise for any window/lag pair that substantially overlaps with
the same informative interval; as window width increases, the lag that best positions the
window over that interval shifts systematically, producing a diagonal ridge. Consistent with this
account, the significance maps show that correlations for saccade frequency and the PCA-
derived component are most pronounced within bands spanning around 0 s lags with ~150-250
s windows and extending to ~160 s lags with ~10-80 s windows (Supplementary Fig. 9a, e).
Oscillation frequency exhibits weaker but similar patterns, peaking around 0-20 s lags for 20-
150 s windows (Supplementary Fig. 9c). Together, these results indicate that neuronal responses
are enhanced following approximately 3-min periods of increased saccadic activity,
corroborating the reported minute-scale coupling effect.
We appreciate for noting the formatting issue in Supplementary Fig. 9e (right panel). We have
corrected the tick marks in the revised figure. In addition, to make the statistical interpretation
more direct, we revised the right panels to display only significance values (−log10(p);
threshold p < 0.05). Together, these additional analyses and figure revisions support the
robustness of the minute-scale effect.
Fig. R2 | Time-resolved correlations between saccadic metrics and neuronal visual
responses across time lag definitions.
a-f, Correlations were recomputed using two additional definitions of the time lag. in (a, c, e),
the lag is defined as the interval between the midpoint of the analysis window and visual
