version, Fig. 3l–m plotted normalized visual responses (each neuron scaled to its own mean
visual response). This normalization inadvertently emphasized on variance differences within
the anterior (pecten-proximal) and posterior (pecten-distal) optic tectum (OT) neurons. Because
posterior OT neurons exhibited larger trial-over-trial variability in visual responses across the
elapsed-since-saccade time (CV: anterior neurons, 0.59; posterior neurons, 0.88), normalization
could give the misleading impression that max > max .
posterior/distal anterior/proximal
In the revision, we re-analyzed the data by comparing raw stimulus-evoked visual responses
(firing rate during the 300 ms stimulus period minus spontaneous baseline). The results show
that anterior neurons (mean ± SEM: 48.04 ± 4.95 spikes/s, n = 33 neurons) exhibited
significantly higher visual responses than posterior neurons (24.24 ± 4.35 spikes/s, n = 24
neurons). To further verify the temporal profiles of these responses, we conducted the suggested

We are particularly encouraged by these new results for two reasons. First, they demonstrate
that anterior (pecten-proximal) neurons exhibit stronger visual responses than posterior (pecten-
distal) neurons, consistent with the estimated glucose concentration gradient and with our
glucose simulations at two locations (Fig. R2). Second, the temporal patterns of neuronal
activity and glucose dynamics remained tightly correlated (Fig. R2). Nonetheless, we
acknowledge that retinal anatomical factors, such as regional ganglion-cell density or sensitivity,
may also contribute. We have now clarified these points and emphasized the temporal dynamics
in the revised text to present the results as objectively as possible.

Additionally, how are glucose levels at the two retinal locations estimated? This methodology
needs to be explicitly described since it's currently unclear how these curves were generated.
Authors: We appreciate the comment highlighting the need to clarify the methodology used to
estimate glucose levels. Pettigrew’s pioneering work in the tawny frogmouth demonstrated that
fluorescein dye can be rapidly propelled ~2–3 mm from the avian pecten within 2 seconds of a
single saccade, whereas during prolonged fixation dye diffusion was minimal (<0.5 mm even
after 120 s). This underscores the inefficiency of passive diffusion mechanisms and highlights
the essential role of saccades in nutrient delivery.
In our study, we aimed to approximate intraocular glucose dynamics in pigeons. Because
outward nutrient transport from the pecten involves a complex three-dimensional process of
diffusion, fluid motion, and metabolic consumption, we simplified the problem into a one-
dimensional diffusion model. In the revised Methods (Line 620-663), we have provided a full
description of this approach. Briefly, glucose dynamics in the vitreous were modeled according
to Fick’s second law, extended with a consumption term and a periodic mechanical component
representing saccadic oscillation. The model was parameterized using published values for
pigeon eye size, blood glucose concentrations, metabolic consumption rates, and diffusion
coefficients (Braun & Sweazea, 2008; Del Amo et al., 2017; Donovan, 1978; Koirala et al.,
2022; Von Eugen et al., 2022).
For simulation, we set the ocular radius to 7 mm (diameter ~13–14 mm) and considered two
retinal sites: a proximal site (1 mm from the pecten) and a distal site (4 mm from the pecten).
Physiological glucose concentrations were set to c1 = 15 mmol/L at the pecten and c2 = 13
mmol/L distally (Braun & Sweazea, 2008). The metabolic consumption rate was estimated from
pigeon brain tissue (27.29 ± 1.57 μmol/100 g/min ≈ 4.55×10−4 mmol/L/s(Von Eugen et al.,
2022), and the diffusion coefficient was derived from corrected water values at 40 °C, reduced
by half to approximate vitreous properties (≈ 4.68 × 10⁻⁴ mm²/s(Koirala et al., 2022)). A
periodic oscillatory term was included based on measured saccade intervals and amplitudes.
This model allowed us to generate time-dependent glucose concentration curves for proximal
and distal retinal locations, capturing the general trends of glucose diffusion influenced by
saccades. While these parameters cannot fully replicate the complex physicochemical
environment of the avian vitreous, the model provides a reasonable theoretical framework to
estimate how glucose availability differs across retinal regions (pecten-proximal vs. pecten-
distal). We also noted in the revised Methods that more precise modeling will require further
fluid-mechanics characterization of the avian vitreous.
Finally, are the other two nuclei, nOPT and nLM, topographically organized?
Authors: Thank you for raising this important point regarding the topographic organization of
the nOPT and nLM. In the case of the nOPT, as noted by Remy and Güntürkün (1991), the
retinal projections are relatively sparse, and retrograde tracing did not reveal a clear or
systematic retinotopic organization. This diffuse and weakly topographic projection pattern
prevents us from reliably inferring receptive field origins from electrode positions, unlike in the
OT where a robust retinotopic map exists. For the nLM, the situation differs somewhat.
Bodnarenko et al. (1988) demonstrated the presence of a retinotopic map in this nucleus.
However, the retinal ganglion cells projecting to the nLM are concentrated in a horizontal band
near the retinal equator, while input from central visual field regions is sparse. These precludes
reliable group comparisons of proximal versus distal representations analogous to those we
conducted in the OT. Taken together, while both nOPT and nLM play important roles in avian
visual processing, the specific anatomical and projection features of OT make it more amenable
to the type of spatially structured analyses we pursued here.
8. It is clear that muscimol injection in the Raphe complex abolishes OSs, but does it also

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
Oscillatory saccades are high frequency (~10-40 Hz) eye movements that often accompany
translational eye saccades in birds. Xu et al. hypothesize that (1) oscillatory saccades are
initiated during visual behaviors that require higher nutrient levels in the retina; (2) these
saccades distribute nutrients (specifically glucose) in the eye, and (3) this increased glucose
distribution improves retinal processing of images.
In support of (1), they show an immediate increase in saccade frequency and oscillation
frequency (although these terms require clarification) upon salient changes in visual input. In
support of (2), they find that intraocular glucose concentrations increase ~3 minutes later and
demonstrate causality by pharmacologically supressing saccades. In support of (3), they record
increased neural responses to visual stimuli in retino-recipient nuclei also ~3 min after periods
of increased saccades. They again provide some evidence for causality through intraocular
glucose injections which increase neural responses, and suppression of saccades which decrease
neural responses.
The neural data, intraocular glucose recording, and simultaneous causal manipulations are
technically challenging and are of particular interest. The main issues revolve around better
contextualizing the specific role of oscillatory saccades, and improving the analysis and
interpretation of temporal correlations between saccades, glucose concentrations, and neural
activity. Overall, the authors provide convincing evidence for a link between oscillatory
saccades, glucose distribution, and visual processing. The result is a fascinating example of
how a neural system solves a challenging metabolic problem, and should therefore be of broad
interest.

validate the temporal coupling between saccadic and neuronal measures.
First, we employed the Pseudosession Method, which tests whether the observed correlations
are genuinely locked to stimulus timing or could emerge from chance alignments of slow
fluctuations in eye movements and neuronal firing. For each neuron, we generated a surrogate
time series of stimulus onsets by randomly shuffling the inter-trial intervals (ITIs) from the

alignment between saccadic history and visual stimuli. As shown in the left panel of
Supplementary Fig. 7, the mean correlation coefficients from the real data (orange line)
systematically deviated from the null distribution (gray shaded area) obtained from the shuffled

stimuli.
Second, we applied the Session Permutation Method, which assesses whether the correlations
are specific to matched neuronal and saccadic metrics from the same recording session, rather
than reflecting shared slow drifts across sessions or animals. Each neuron’s recording (n = 54)

significant negative correlations were observed at the second-scale and significant positive
correlations at the minute-scale, confirming that the temporal relationships we observed are not
artifacts of overlapping saccade histories or slow session-level drifts.

Authors: Thank you so much for this important comment. We have clarified the distinction
between the two timescales in the revised manuscript.
The second-scale negative correlation (< 6 s) is directly supported by both the neuronal
response data and our biophysical simulation (Fig. 3). Neuronal visual responses increased
progressively with longer stimulus-saccade intervals after each saccade (Fig. 3). Additional
analyses of the latest saccade duration further revealed that the longer saccades significantly
enhanced subsequent neuronal visual responses, as your following comments suggested (see
details later). These findings support a local convective–diffusive relaxation process triggered
by fluid perturbations induced by a single saccade. Consistent with this interpretation, our
simulation based on Fick’s second law predicted that intraocular glucose concentration re-
equilibrates within a few seconds over inner-retinal distances, matching the timescale of the
observed neuronal response dynamics. Thus, the second-scale modulation likely reflects a brief
adjustment of nutrient gradients following eye motion.
In contrast, the minute-scale positive correlation (~3-4 min) represents a slow cumulative effect
in which saccades, through fluid-dynamic agitation, enhance glucose diffusion relative to its
metabolic consumption, gradually improving nutrient availability in the avascular avian retina.
Repetitive saccadic eye movements increase the effective diffusivity of glucose and promote
mild convection, producing a slowly accumulating imbalance between metabolic consumptions
and nutrient delivery, and consequently a gradual rise in intraocular glucose concentration. This
long-term process aligns closely with the delayed enhancement of intraocular glucose levels
and neuronal responsiveness observed in the study.
Together, these findings support a dual-timescale mechanism: a rapid convective–diffusive
recovery that occurs within seconds after each saccade, and a slow cumulative enhancement of
metabolic support that builds up over minutes through repeated saccades. We have now clarified
that the slow correlation most likely reflects a cumulative metabolic process, whereas the fast
correlation reflects a transient, mechanically induced modulation, indicating that distinct
mechanisms rather than a single diffusion process spanning both timescales.

measured downstream in retino-recipient areas, could post-saccadic suppression play a role?
Could mechanical disturbance affect RGC firing?

mesencephali (nLM) exhibited a characteristic pattern of pre-saccadic inhibition followed by
post-saccadic enhancement lasting serval hundred milliseconds. This temporal profile contrasts
sharply with the present findings, in which neuronal visual responses exhibited gradual, multi-
second modulations following the latest saccade onset.

Notably, to minimize potential contamination from peri-saccadic modulations, we implemented
exclusion criteria in the present analyses. As detailed in the Methods, we first quantified the

identifying the time point at which firing rate consistently returned to baseline stability. All
visual response data failing within these modulation windows were subsequently excluded,
ensuring that the analysis focused exclusively on stable fixation periods. Visual response to the
300-ms grating probe were calculated by subtracting a baseline defined as the mean
spontaneous firing rate during a 300-ms window aligned to the probe timing relative to the
preceding saccade. Thus, we are confident that the second-scale effects analyzed in this study,

∼
hundred milliseconds, and all data during saccades were excluded from the analysis, we

diffuse and reach retinal cells, both saccade duration and the interval from the latest saccade
should influence neuronal responses.
To disentangle the effects of these correlated factors, we performed correlation analyses across
54 neurons (Fig. 2), applying linear regression models to control for one parameter while
examining the other. The population analyses still revealed significant positive correlations
(saccade duration: r = 0.05, p < 0.001; oscillatory cycle count: r = 0.05, p < 0.001; multiple
linear regression; Fig. R8a, b) between the time from the latest saccade and the corresponding
visual responses when controlling for saccade duration and oscillatory cycle count, respectively.
Similarly, significant positive correlations (saccade duration: r = 0.37, p = 0.04; oscillatory
count: r = 0.02, p = 0.04; multiple linear regression; Fig. R8 c, d) were observed between
saccade duration, oscillatory cycle count and visual responses when controlling for the time
from the latest saccade.
Fig. R8. Partial correlation between normalized visual response and features of the last
saccade.
a, Relationship between normalized visual response and time since the last saccade, controlling

multiple linear regression. b, Relationship between normalized visual response and time since
the last saccade, controlling for the oscillatory cycle count of the last saccade. r = 0.05, p <
0.001, multiple linear regression. c, d, Relationship between normalized visual response and
saccade duration (c, r = 0.37, p = 0.04, multiple linear regression), and oscillatory cycle count
(d, r = 0.02, p = 0.04, multiple linear regression), controlling for time since the last saccade.
Regarding the intrasaccadic frequency of oscillations, we note that this measure corresponds
more closely to the intrasaccadic frequency as defined in the revised Figure 1. The intrasaccadic
frequency reflects the oscillatory cycle frequency within individual saccade bursts and
remained stable across different visual contexts, suggesting it may represent an intrinsic
property of saccades rather than a modifiable factor. Therefore, it was not included in the
present correlation analysis.
These findings support the interpretation that the short-timescale effects arise from oscillatory
mechanical agitation that transiently facilitates rapid glucose delivery to metabolically active
retinal regions. We have incorporated these new results into the revised manuscript, which we
believe provide additional support for the short-timescale hypothesis.
- The authors don't mention oxygen diffusion at all, even though is is a previously proposed role
for oscillatory saccades. Could other nutrients such as oxygen diffuse at different rates?
Authors: Thank you very much for highlighting the potential role of oxygen diffusion. While
our study primarily measured glucose dynamics, we agree that other nutrients, particularly
oxygen, could contribute to the functional role of saccades. Oxygen diffusion and blood flow
are indeed essential for retinal metabolism. Wingstrand et al. reported the crucial role of the
pecten in maintaining intraocular oxygen supply (Wingstrand & Munk, 1965). In anesthetized
pigeons, they observed an oxygen partial pressure gradient from the pecten to the retinal
periphery, and vessel occlusion caused a sharp drop in oxygen tension accompanied by retinal
degeneration. Wallman et al. further proposed that saccadic oscillations may facilitate the
diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from the avian pecten to the retina. However, direct
experimental evidence supporting this hypothesis remains limited.
In the present study, we directly monitored intraocular glucose dynamics using a continuous
glucose monitoring (CGM) system and found a temporal correlation between glucose
fluctuations and saccade activity. We have now added a statement in the Discussion
acknowledging that oxygen (and potentially other metabolic substrates) may also play a role
and that differences in their diffusion and transport properties could modulate their
physiological relevance. We explicitly state that our conclusions are based on glucose-
dependent evidence and do not exclude possible contributions from oxygen or other nutrients.
Future work may test whether saccades similarly modulate intraocular oxygen levels and visual
sensitivity.
- Can the causal manipulations provide some insight? What is the temporal relationship between
the increase in intraocular glucose concentration caused by injection, and the increase in neural
response? The Raphe inhibition experiments demonstrate a 3-4 min lag between decreased
saccades and decreased glucose concentration, but what is the time lag with the neural response?
Authors: We sincerely thank you for this valuable suggestion, which has helped us improve
both the precision and the mechanistic clarity of the revised manuscript.
Following the direct D-glucose injection, our analysis showed that the enhancement of neuronal
responses was very rapid, with a latency of only 0.25 minutes (15 seconds, p < 0.05).
Conversely, inhibiting glucose transport with Bay-876 resulted in a decrease in neuronal
responses with a latency of 1.25 minutes (p < 0.05). These findings confirm that neuronal
activity is indeed highly sensitive to local glucose availability. We have clarified the
methodology for this analysis in the revised Methods section:
"To assess post-injection dynamics of neuronal activity, data were aligned to the injection time
and analyzed in 0.5-min windows. Activity in each window was z-score normalized to the pre-
injection baseline (outliers >3 standardized MAD excluded). The latency of significant change
was defined as the median time of the first window differing from baseline."
Regarding the Raphe complex inhibition experiment, our data demonstrate a 3-4 minute lag
from the reduction in saccadic metrics to the decline in intraocular glucose concentrations (Fig.
5e) . To address the specific question about the lag with the neuronal response, our new analyses
revealed a consistent delay of about 4.3 minutes from the muscimol injection to the attenuation
of neuronal responses. Crucially, we also determined there was a 0.5-0.7 min delay between the
injection and the actual suppression of eye movements (Supplementary Fig. 3f). Therefore,
when accounting for this initial pharmacological delay on eye movements, the resulting lag
between the cessation of saccades and the subsequent decline in neuronal responses is
approximately 3.6-3.8 minutes. The close correspondence between these two key time lags: the
3.6–3.8-minute delay from reduced saccades to neuronal responses inhibition and the 3-4-
minute delay from reduced saccades to decreased intraocular glucose concentrations (Fig. 5e),
suggest that within approximately 3-4 minutes after saccades cease, both glucose supply
disruption and neuronal activity decline occur nearly simultaneously.
4. Some conclusions are overstated
- Lines 99-101. "These findings indicate that attention-driven oscillatory saccades in birds
enhance glucose mobilization from the pecten oculi to the retina, thereby boosting nutrient
supply during social information gathering" This conclusion is overstated at this point since
causality has not yet been established. It is plausible at this point that viewing a salient stimulus
causes other changes in attention and arousal that lead to both increased glucose circulation
(with a delay) and increased saccade rates. A similar comment applies to lines 113-116.
Authors: We thank you so much for this important comment. We agree that the original wording
overstated the causal link between oscillatory saccades and glucose mobilization prior to the
results of pharmacological manipulations. At this part, our data demonstrate a temporal
association between saccade rates and intraocular glucose fluctuations, but do not yet establish
a direct causal mechanism. Accordingly, we have revised the text at both locations to present
our interpretation more cautiously, emphasizing that saccades are correlated with, rather than
directly responsible for, enhanced glucose mobilization during salient visual events.
- Line 284 - "Meanwhile, avian visual responses are not only sustained, but dynamically
optimized to efficiently process salient and intricate visual stimuli by enhancing retinal energy
availability" What does this sentence mean? I don't believe the authors distinguish between the
effects of oscillatory saccades on sustained vs. transient neural responses. Similarly, what is the
evidence for "precise shaping of retinal function" -- the authors do not demonstrate sharpening
of receptive fields, for example.
Authors: Thank you so much for the valuable comment. We apologize that the original wording
(“sustained” and “precise shaping”) was misleading and did not accurately reflect our results.
We do not distinguish between sustained and transient neuronal responses, nor do we provide
evidence for receptive-field sharpening. Our findings instead show that avian saccades are
closely coupled with fluctuations in intraocular glucose levels, suggesting a mechanism that
helps maintain retinal energy availability during visual processing. Accordingly, we have
revised the statement to read more conservatively, noting that saccades may support retinal
glucose supply, thereby facilitating visual processing.
- Line 292 "Our findings provide novel insights into the critical role of avian oscillatory
saccades and extend their significance beyond basic visual scanning to metabolic and functional
optimization." Previous studies cited don't seem to suggest that the oscillatory component of
avian saccades is used for visual scanning/gaze orienting. How could a fast ~30 Hz oscillation
possibly achieve scanning? "Moreover, they raise broader implications regarding the role of
eye movements in maintaining retinal health, enhancing attentional performance, and
optimizing visual function across species." What are these broader implications exactly?
Authors: We fully understand your concerns and appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point.
First, in pigeons, all saccades are inherently oscillatory(Wallman & Letelier, 1993). The
oscillatory component is an intrinsic feature of each saccade rather than a distinct type of eye
movement. Each saccadic eye movement therefore combines a positional shift with embedded
high-frequency (~30Hz) oscillations in pigeons (Nye, 1969). As in mammals, one function of
a saccade in birds is to reorient gaze toward a new location of interest. We apologize that the
term “oscillatory saccades” in the previous version may have been misleading. In the revised
manuscript, we have clarified three properties of avian saccades in Figure 1. Among them, the
~30 Hz oscillatory frequency itself, as correctly note, is too fast to serve a visual scanning or
gaze orientation, which are accomplished by the overall saccadic displacement.
Second, during saccade, visual input is likely blurred, akin to viewing a scene through a rapidly
shaking camera. However, these blurred images are not normally processed by the brain
because of saccadic visual suppression. Previous studies have demonstrated that, in pigeons,
activity along the primary visual pathways, from the nOPT to higher visual centers, is strongly
suppressed during saccades by corollary discharge signals from the Raphe complex (Yan Yang
et al., 2008), paralleling the phenomenon of saccadic suppression in humans that prevents
perception of motion blur during rapid eye movements.
Taken together, these observations suggest that saccadic eye movements in pigeons may serve
dual roles: beyond their gaze orienting function, they may also contribute to maintaining retinal
health and metabolic homeostasis through movement-coupled perfusion and nutrient-delivery
mechanisms. We have revised the corresponding text to clarify these distinctions and to better
articulate the broader physiological implications.

Authors: We appreciate your careful reading. To clarify, birds indeed produce saccades that
inherently contain oscillatory components, rather than distinct “oscillatory” and “non-

Wallman and Letelier (1993) noted that “in chickens and pigeons it is clear that all saccades

“a typical saccadic eye movement consists of several oscillatory cycles occurring at a frequency
of approximately 18–44 Hz.” We have carefully revised the manuscript, especially in the
Introduction and Results sections to make this point explicit and to avoid unintended
implication that only certain saccades are oscillatory.

Authors: We appreciate your insightful feedback on the definition and interpretation of our
behavioral metrics. As noted, “saccade frequency” (or rates of saccades) and “oscillation
frequency” are central to our study but were not clearly defined in the original submission.
Saccades are rapid, oscillatory bursts of eye movements at periodic intervals in pigeons (Nye,
1969; Wallman & Letelier, 1993). To capture their temporal organization, we included a
detailed definition in the revised manuscript: 1) Saccade frequency: the number of detected
saccades per analysis window, representing the rate of oscillatory episodes occurred. 2)
Oscillation frequency: the total number of oscillatory cycles embedded within all saccades in
an analysis window, representing the overall temporal density of oscillatory activity. 3)
Intrasaccadic frequency: the reciprocal of each oscillatory cycle duration, reflecting the
oscillation rate within a saccadic burst (typically 20–30 Hz in our data, consistent with Nye
(1969). The revised Fig. 1c now systematically illustrated theses three frequency-related
metrics, saccade frequency (F ), oscillation frequency (F ), and intrasaccadic frequency
sac osci
(F ) along with their relation to the established characteristics of avian saccadic eye
intra
movements in the literature. The updated figure also shows how these metrics vary across
different visual conditions in pigeons (Fig. 1d, e). These new results demonstrate that only
saccade frequency and oscillation frequency changed significantly across viewing conditions,
thereby providing a clearer foundation for subsequent analyses and interpretation.
Regarding the lower baseline frequencies, the higher “oscillation frequencies” (~20-30 hz)
reported in the earlier studies correspond to intrasaccadic frequency, not to the oscillation
frequency as defined in this study. Our intrasaccadic frequency (20–30 Hz) is fully consistent
with prior findings (Letelier et al., 1999; Nye, 1969; Yang Yang et al., 2008), while the saccade
frequency values closely match those in previous reports (Yan Yang et al., 2008). Finally, the
0.04 Hz value reported after muscimol injection represents the oscillation frequency, not the
intrasaccadic frequency within a burst. This low value reflects the elimination of saccadic
oscillation events following Raphe inactivation. We have clarified this distinction in the revised
Results section.

6. Fig 1d - What do individual data points represent and how are they calculated (e.g. over
what time period is the response and baseline calculated)?
Authors: Thank you for your attention to the details of our data representation. In the previous
version, Fig. 1d showed data from an example animal. Each data point represented the
normalized saccade frequency (x-axis) and oscillation frequency (y-axis) within a 1-minute
time window. Frequencies were calculated using a moving-window approach, in which a 1-
minute window was slid across the entire experimental timeline in 0.1-minute (6-second) steps,
and frequency values were determined by counting the number of events occurring within the
1-minute window centered on each time point (30 seconds before and 30 seconds after). All
frequency values were normalized relative to a baseline period defined as the 30-minute gray-
screen phase preceding social video playback, with the mean baseline frequency used as the
reference.
Per your and other reviewers’ constructive comments, we have clarified the quantification of
avian saccadic metrics across distinct visual conditions and compared the relationships between
saccade frequency and oscillation frequency in the revised version. Each data point now
represents the normalized saccade frequency (x-axis) and oscillation frequency (y-axis)
calculated within discrete, non-overlapping 1-minute time windows (Fig. 1e). To illustrate how
saccades were evoked by visual stimuli, we reordered the presentation of results to begin with
“simple” luminance transitions between light and dark screens, followed by the viewing of
social mating videos. Accordingly, the population responses of saccadic activity and intraocular
glucose fluctuations during social video viewing were averaged across four animals and
normalized to the preceding 30-minute gray-screen phase (Fig. 1q).
7. Fig. 3j - What is the model?
Authors: Thank you for your question concerning the model, which is important in the study.
The model implanted in Fig. 3j is a conceptual diffusion-consumption framework designed to
simulate intraocular glucose concentration dynamics under the influence of saccades. We
adopted this simplified approach to estimate how saccadic oscillations might modulate glucose
accessibility at different retinal loci.
A full description of the model is now included in the revised Methods (Lines 620–663). The
model is based on Fick’s second law of diffusion, extended to include a glucose consumption
term and a periodic mechanical perturbation term to represent saccadic effects. Anatomical and
physiological parameters (e.g. ocular radius, baseline glucose concentrations, metabolic
consumption rates, and diffusion coefficients; (Braun & Sweazea, 2008; Del Amo et al., 2017;
Donovan, 1978; Koirala et al., 2022; Von Eugen et al., 2022)) were drawn from published data
or experimentally measured values. Two retinal distances were modeled: one proximal (~1 mm
from the pecten) and one more distal (~4 mm from the pecten). The simulation yields time-
dependent glucose concentration curves at each location, illustrating the relative effect of
saccadic activity on nutrient distribution and spatial gradients. While the model does not capture
the full complexity of three-dimensional vitreous fluid flow and biochemical interactions, it
provides a quantitative framework for comparing glucose dynamics between regions and
assessing the potential contribution of saccadic eye movements to nutrient delivery. We have
updated the legend of Fig. 3 and added a detailed description in the Methods to clarify the
model’s construction and underlying assumptions, which we believe will enhance clarity and
interpretability for readers.
8. Fig. 4c - What is the color scale? How can neurons have a response of -30 sp/s? Also please
add start & ending trial numbers.
Authors: The color scale in Fig. 4C represents baseline-corrected neuronal firing rates (spikes/s).
In this study, a 300-ms grating motion served as a probe to assess neuronal visual responses,
and firing rates were computed in 50-ms bins. Baselines were defined as average spontaneous
firing rates during saccade intervals without probes, aligned to the time point of prior probe.
Visual responses to the grating motion were obtained by subtracting this baseline from the
probe-evoked firing rate. Accordingly, negative values indicate suppression below baseline
firing, whereas positive values indicate excitatory responses to the grating motion. In
accordance with your suggestion, we have added annotations for the starting and ending trial
(probe) numbers in the revised figure.
9. Line 171 - What does "A 5.00-6.00" refer to?
Authors: Thank you for raising this point. "A 5.00–6.00" refers to stereotaxic coordinates of the
pigeon brain. Our coordinate system follows the standards established by Karten and Hodos
(1967), which remains the reference for avian brain anatomy. Here, "A" stands for anterior,
indicating a position along the anterior–posterior axis relative to the reference point (bregma).
The values 5.00–6.00 denote the distance in millimeters (mm) from bregma. In avian
neuroanatomy, bregma (the intersection of the sagittal suture and the mid-plane of the ear canals)
is conventionally used as the origin for stereotaxic coordinates, from which anterior (A),
posterior (P), dorsal (D), ventral (V), medial (M), and lateral (L) directions are defined. We
apologize for the lack of explicit unit labeling in the manuscript. In the revision, we have added
“mm” when these coordinates first appear, included a brief explanation of the notation, and
cited the stereotaxic atlas for clarity.
10. What is the effect of muscimol injections in the Raphe nucleus on both regular saccades
and oscillatory saccades? It is unclear if effects are due to suppression of the oscillatory
component specifically.
Authors: We appreciate for the important question. In pigeons, each saccade comprises of a
burst of oscillatory cycles. The Raphe complex is critical for generating the oscillatory
component. Muscimol injections into the Raphe complex selectively suppressed the oscillatory
activity. Thus, Raphe complex inactivation does specifically disrupt oscillatory dynamics,
supported by our previous lesion studies (Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang Yang et al., 2008). We
have clarified this point in the revised manuscript.
11. Discussion - Studies have demonstrated dramatic differences in eye movements in head
fixed vs. unrestrained birds. See Land 2015 and Gioanni 1988. Are oscillations equally
important when the head is free to move? Have they been demonstrated in both head fixation
and free motion?
Authors: We appreciate you for raising this important point and for highlighting the relevant
references. Eye movements during optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) can indeed differ between
head-fixed and unrestrained conditions, especially in the gain relationship between the slow
phase of OKN and the stimulus velocity. Nevertheless, the oscillatory component of saccades
has been shown to be a robust and consistent feature across behavioral conditions. Multiple
studies employing high-temporal resolution methods, including search coil system and EOG
recordings, have demonstrated that oscillations occur during both spontaneous saccades and the
quick phases of OKN in head-free as well as head-fixed birds (Gioanni, 1988; Land, 2015;
Wallman & Letelier, 1993; Xiao et al., 2023; Yan Yang et al., 2008; Yang Yang et al., 2008). To
further illustrate this point, we have added a supplementary video (Supplementary Video 6)
showing saccades with oscillatory components in a head-free pigeon, observed both when the
head was still and when it was moving. We also compared stimulus-driven saccades during
viewing of light, dark, and gray screens, as well as during presentation of social mating videos
(updated Fig. 1). In the present study, head fixation was applied to ensure stable recordings of
well-isolated single-neuron activity. These methodological considerations have been clarified
in the revised Methods section.
12. Line 274 - Reference 50 doesn't contain any mention of the Raphe complex. It would be
helpful to clarify the proposed role of the Raphe complex in generation of regular saccades vs.
oscillatory saccades.
Authors: We thank you for the careful observation. You are correct that Reference 50 does not
explicitly mention the raphe complex. Instead, it provides a broad review of brainstem
mechanisms underlying saccade control, particularly the role of omnipause neurons (OPNs).
The Raphe complex, especially the nucleus raphe interpositus (RIP), contains OPNs that fire
tonically during fixation but pause during saccades in all directions, thereby gating saccade.
In birds, virtually all saccades contain oscillatory components (Wallman & Letelier, 1993),
even when the head is free to move (see new Supplementary Video 6). Our previous lesion studies
have shown that disruption of the Raphe complex eliminate saccadic oscillations dramatically
(Yan Yang et al., 2008). Thus, the Raphe complex plays a key role in generating avian saccades.
In light of this clarification, we have removed the original citation and revised the text to clearly
describe the specific features of avian saccades and the role of the Raphe complex.
